newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Minority govt seen mildly negative for Irish mkts.
newsitem.headline: Minority govt seen mildly negative for Irish mkts.

text.p: With counting drawing to a close in Ireland's election on Sunday, a minority coalition government looked the most likely outcome, a mildly negative result for Irish financial markets, analysts said.

But this should be offset by the fact that the main opposition party, Fianna Fail, and its right-wing Progressive Democrats ally, should be just a few seats short of an overall majority, giving them a good chance of forming a stable government.

"Whereas this is the worst possible outcome for the markets, which would have preferred to see either coalition get in, it is tempered by the fact that they have a near majority," said Eoin Fahy, economist at Ulster Bank.

With 156 out of the 166 parliamentary seats counted, Fianna Fail looked on course to win 77-79 seats with the Progressive Democrats likely to hold onto four of their eight seats after an electoral mauling.
Together with the support of Independents, at least three of whom have been affiliated to Fianna Fail in the past, the two parties should be able to achieve a working majority, analysts said.
"I don't think the markets will exactly be celebrating on Monday but I don't think there will be any negative reaction," Oliver Mangan, bond economist at AIB Group Treasury, told Reuters.

"At least after this election we have a fairly clear idea, unlike the last three elections, where we are going to get the next government from...and there is a basis there for stable government," he said.

Analysts said that even if the government was vulnerable to pressure from independent politicians on local issues from time to time, it was unlikely to come under pressure on the economic policy front.

"I would have thought you were looking at a reasonably stable government with a lifetime of two to three years with all sorts of controversies arising from time to time but few enough of them about economic policies and in particular Economic and monetary union (EMU)," said Ulster Bank's Fahy.

Economists said there was unlikely to be a major adverse reaction when Irish financial markets opened on Monday, especially as a Fianna Fail/Progressive Democrat government would not result in any real change to the broad thrust of macro-economic policy.

"I don't expect there to be much impact. The only reason I think there might be any is because the markets have been very turbulent for the last three or four weeks and it is possible that if there are speculators out there, waiting to sell the Irish pound, it might be a signal to do so," Fahy said.

the Irish currency has taken a beating in recent weeks in a sell-off prompted by speculation that the punt will have to enter the single European currency at a much lower rate against the German mark than currently prevails.
Riada's Dan McLaughlin pointed out that while the result was "messy", other issues would have more impact on the market in coming days.
"It is not positive for the market but it's likely to be dwarfed by a number of issues looming such as domestic interest rate concerns and the possibility of an EMU delay."

Analysts also noted that while there might be a period of uncertainty until the new government's position on the Irish pound becomes clear, the weak showing of the Progressive Democrats had reduced their ability to influence Irish policy on EMU.

The Progressive Democrats had expressed reservations about the Irish pound joining a single currency without sterling, putting them at odds with Fianna Fail which is committed to joining EMU in the first wave.
"Their ability to have a major impact in that sense is greatly diminished by their performance in the election," said AIB's Mangan.
